doc.title: Frank Foster — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: War, marijuana and boredom in Korea
summary: He saw no combat but heard gunfire nightly, disliked the army, and recalls smoking marijuana grown in the fields.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: Did you see combat?
No, I didn’t see combat, but every night we could hear small arms fire going, machine guns.
What did the experience of being, and I guess you’re getting to this, but how did it feel being in a war? How did it affect you as a human being?

It didn’t feel good at all. I did not like it. I did not like the Korean countryside. I hated the army experience of getting up early in the morning and having a long day, a long hard day, and finally getting to bed at night and getting -- we’d get a pass to go into a local village. All you could smell was fertilizer when you went into the village. It seemed like our only recreation was going into the village and uh --
The great “uh.”
Yeah, the great “uh.”
Uh.

We did discover marijuana stalks growing in the fields, marijuana stalks that grew to six feet in height. We’d cut them and pluck the branches off the main stalk. We’d hang them upside down to let the essence flow to the leaves. Then we’d fill an empty cake box, like if somebody’s mother sent them a fruitcake. As soon as we finished the fruitcake, we’d fill the cake box with dried marijuana leaves. That was our best recreation.
What did you do, look at them?
I’ll let you guess [laughs].
Let me make the inference?
I’ll let you make the call.
You’ll let me induct, deduct, and redact, okay [laughs].
We would empty cigarettes. We didn’t have what you call cigarette papers. We would buy conventional cigarettes.
Was it boring?
Huh?
Was it boring? Did you think it would end?
Strangely enough it was not boring. I though it would never end, yeah.
You thought it seemed endless.
It wasn’t boring, because -- we did have some music to listen to. We won a tape recorder in a contest. We would record our own music on this tape recorder, and we would --
Were the units segregated?

No, no. The training unit at Camp Roberts California, was segregated. The army on an overall basis was integrated by that time in the early 1950s, but the integrated status hadn’t gotten to Camp Roberts yet. So we trained as a segregated unit, but as soon as I got to Japan everything was totally integrated. All organizations, band, every area was totally integrated.
